title: Core B - Renewal Ocular Imaging Core Vision Research
text: III. Ocular Imaging Core Project Summary The Ocular Imaging Core will provide a variety of imaging modalities to the investigators involved in this P30 Cole Eye Vision Research Core. The module includes live animal (in vivo) imaging with slit lamp and fundus photography, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) and optical coherence tomography (OCT). It also supports tissue and cellular imaging (ex vivo) support, providing training and assistance with routine and specialized tissue fixation techniques, paraffin and plastic tissue embedding, sectioning (paraffin, Cryo and plastic/resin) and staining for immunohistochemistry. Microscope imaging techniques include bright field, dark field, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal and electron microscopy. It also provides help and advice with the morphometric analysis of generated images. Access to this core module will support NEI R01 funded investigators, help newly recruited investigators obtain data for NEI R01 grant submissions, foster collaborative interactions between RO1-funded investigators and newly recruited investigators, attract investigators from other departments to research on the visual system and be a valuable departmental resource in attracting additional vision scientists to our program as we expand our research faculty.

title: Public Health Insurance and Mortality Among People with Disabilities
text: Little is known about the mortality rates and causes of death experienced by people living with disabilities, the importance of various factors in exacerbating high mortality rates, or the role of insurance in improving care and health for this population. This study will characterize all-cause and cause-specific mortality while estimating how Medicaid expansion and automatic enrollment affect coverage, healthcare access and utilization, and mortality. Findings will help identify the populations and health needs for which evidence-based screening, prevention, treatment, and disease-management services should be prioritized to improve health and reduce preventable mortality among people with disabilities.

title: Diurnal control of memory allocation by the circadian gene Per1
text:
Nearly all animals, including humans, are governed by an internal circadian clock that regulates biological
processes, including memory formation, across the 24h day/night cycle. Both non-pathological aging and
Alzheimer’s diseases are accompanied by impairments in both memory and circadian rhythmicity, but the
connection between these age-related deficits is currently unclear. This proposal will examine an important
circadian gene that may underlie age-related impairments in both memory and circadian rhythmicity and may
represent a novel therapeutic target for improving cognition in aging individuals.

title: Interpreting and Deploying Genomic Information During Animal Development
text:
Many human diseases, from cancer to diabetes, can be caused by the misregulation of genes
due to mutations in the DNA binding sites for key transcription factors. This project aims to
understand at a high-resolution and mechanistic level, how transcription factors combinatorially
recognize these binding sites and recruit the correct sets of co-regulators to accurately regulate
their target genes during animal development. Particular attention is paid to transcription factors
that are members of large DNA binding families, such as homeodomain proteins, that have very
similar DNA binding specificities on their own, yet carry out distinct functions in vivo.

title: Project 2: Integrating race, ethnicity, and genomic ancestry across GENIE to understand genetic and environmental contributions to pan-cancer risk, prognosis, and outcomes
text:
PROJECT 2 NARRATIVE 
Despite significant advances in cancer biology and clinical oncology, genetic ancestry-based differences in cancer outcomes remain a long-standing challenge. We propose to investigate how genetic ancestry contributes to cancer outcomes in the largest publicly available registry of the broad cancer patient population.

title: Identifying chromatin factors essential for DNA repair using a novel high-throughput screening methodology
text: (See instructions): Mammalian cells are continually exposed to environmental toxicants including UV-radiation and various sources of ionizing radiation (IR) threatening genomic integrity, leading to an increased risk of cancer and neurodegenerative disease. Given our constant exposure to environmental toxicants, elucidating fundamental principles of genome integrity maintenance is critical for developing therapeutic interventions for a host of age-related pathologies. In recent years, several chromatin-based events have been shown to be critical mediators of an effective DNA damage response (DDR), however the lack of high-throughput screening methodologies have significantly hampered the identification of chromatin factors essential for DNA repair. To address this, this proposal will use a newly developed high-throughput screening methodology, coupled with a cDNA library of predicted chromatin interactors (“ChromORFeome”), to identify novel chromatin factors involved in DNA repair. During the R00 phase of this proposal, the candidate will build upon the data developed during the mentored (K99) research phase to further understand the importance of a newly identified chromatin-interacting protein, ZNF280A, for the repair of DNA damage. Specifically, this proposal will seek to understand how ZNF280A is regulated in response to DNA damage. This aim will use a range of complementary approaches including protein biochemistry, phospho-proteomics, and mutagenesis analysis to map post-translational modifications on ZNF280A and determine their importance for regulating the function of ZNF280A in DNA double-strand break repair (Aim 1). In addition, this proposal will build upon preliminary data generated during the K99 phase of the proposal which identified novel protein-protein interaction networks, to determine mechanistically how ZNF280A orchestrates DNA repair (Aim 2A) and ascertain whether this contributes to therapy resistance in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), where increased expression of ZNF280A correlates with significantly poorer outcome in patients (Aim 2B). In addition, very little is known about how chromatin structure and function is re-established following DNA repair. To begin to explore this, the proposal will utilize our recently developed high-throughput screening methodology to identify novel chromatin factors involved in the late stages of DNA repair and mechanistically characterize how these factors orchestrate the re-setting of chromatin architecture following DNA damage repair (Aim 3). These experimental aims will provide the candidate with data for an early independent publication and preliminary data for R series

title: The Interplay between Genetics and Aerobic Exercise to Slow Parkinson's disease (GEARS) Trial
text:
This project will determine the disease altering properties of high intensity aerobic exercise through the
systematic examination of 250 individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD) who participate in a 12-month
community-based cycling program compared to a historical control group of 125 individuals with PD with
identical outcome metrics. The role of genetics in exercise and disease progression will be examined by
developing a prognostic model in which genetic burden, determined through the calculation of a PD polygenic
risk score, is a key factor. Identifying the potential role genetics may have in modulating the disease altering
potential of exercise will advance PD understanding and accelerate development of a personalized medicine
approach to PD exercise prescription.

title: Technology Training and Dissemation
text: Limited mobility due to conditions like osteoarthritis, neuromuscular diseases, and limb loss affects millions of individuals, at enormous personal and societal cost. The Mobilize Center is providing much needed tools and exerting a substantial, positive influence on the large community of researchers who study mobility limitations. Training and dissemination are necessary to ensure the Center’s technology makes an impact across many different biomedical research areas. We will build on our well-established infrastructure and experiences to continue and expand our training and dissemination program. Our aims for training and dissemination include the following: 1. Enhance our integrated communications infrastructure to promote the Center’s resources and activities. The Mobilize Center will continue to engage individuals across the biomedical research community using a variety of channels, including websites, social media, and newsletters. 2. Organize introductory workshops and symposia at major conferences to expose 750+ individuals to our software tools and best practices. We will organize two introductory hands-on tutorials and one symposium at conferences each year to broaden awareness of the Mobilize Center software and resources and to advance the use of machine learning and biomechanics in biomedical research. 3. Provide in-depth training on our software tools to 200+ researchers via intensive, multi-day workshops. We will run one in-person workshop each year; these interactive events will provide participants with focused, expert support to enhance their use of our software tools. 4. Expand our online resources to guide biomedical researchers. Our websites provide an extensive range of resources, including our software packages; wiki-based user guides; interactive, web-based tutorials that walk users through using our coding resources; and video recordings of workshop and conference presentations. 5. Train researchers to run Digital Health Days to collect quantitative biomechanics data at scale. Our team has pioneered “Digital Health Days”, where we rapidly collect large-scale data with OpenCap. We will train other researchers to emulate our Digital Health Days, expanding the amount of quantitative biomechanics data available for research. Together these training and dissemination efforts will empower the movement science and rehabilitation communities to easily and effectively collect, analyze, and gain insights from quantitative biomechanics data

title: Causes and Consequences of Adenosine Signaling in Pancreatic Cancer
text:
This research project aims to investigate the causes and consequences of adenosine-mediated
immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer (PDAC) and explore the efficacy of adenosine-targeted therapies. By
understanding the mechanisms underlying adenosine signaling in the PDAC tumor microenvironment, the
study will contribute to the fundamental knowledge about the complex interactions between cancer and
immune cells in solid tumors. The potential development of adenosine-targeted therapies could have a positive
impact on improving treatment options and outcomes for patients with pancreatic cancer, ultimately enhancing
health and reducing illness and disability associated with this challenging disease.

title: Microscopy and Animal Phenotyping
text: Resource/Service Core: Microscopy and Animal Phenotyping Module Abstract The Microscopy and Animal Phenotyping Module will continue to provide equipment, infrastructural support, expertise, and technical assistance to vision scientists in order to enable detailed, quantitative imaging of cells and tissues, as well as equipment and support for structural and functional assessment of the visual system in vivo. This state-of-the-art facility includes several pieces of high-end hardware for image and data collection, dedicated analysis workstations, and the expertise needed to support and enhance ongoing research and explore new research questions posed by vision scientists. Facility operations will include: 1) maintaining and servicing the equipment, 2) managing usage of the equipment, 3) educating investigators on the capabilities of the equipment, 4) advising investigators on the design of imaging experiments for vision research projects, 5) providing training on the proper usage of the equipment, and 6) helping researchers collect, process and analyze high quality microscopy and visual function data for both current and future applications. The specific services and technologies provided within the Microscopy and Animal Phenotyping Facility are: a) cell and tissue processing, labeling, and immunocytochemistry, b) light and fluorescent microscopy, c) laser scanning confocal microscopy, d) multiphoton microscopy and time-lapse imaging, e) slit lamp imaging and in vivo confocal microscopy, f) optical coherence tomography (OCT), angiography, autofluorescence imaging (BAF), infrared imaging (IR), and fundus imaging, g) electroretinography (ERG/PERG/VEP), h) behavioral testing (optokinetic response, looming object, and pupillometry), and i) quantitative image and data analysis. Overall, the Microscopy and Animal Phenotyping Module will support a range of imaging technologies for participating investigators, and facilitate easy access to equipment, training and technical support that will expand experimental capabilities, open up new research directions, and result in more cost-effective, time- efficient, and rigorous imaging studies. An additional goal is to facilitate collaborative studies using these cutting-edge imaging techniques among vision scientists at UTSW and with other outside institutions.

title: Large-scale transcriptome and epigenome association analysis across multiple traits
text:
The Million Veteran Program (MVP) constitutes the largest and most comprehensive biobank in the world,
including multi-ancestry genetic data from more than 650,000 Veterans and dense electronic health records that
fully captures the clinical characteristics of each participant. MVP provides a unique opportunity to perform large-
scale genetic analyses and further our understanding of Precision Psychiatry across multiple traits and diseases.
Here, we propose to leverage MVP data, integrate them with brain molecular profiling data, and perform a
comprehensive analysis to investigate the functional roles of variants associated with serious mental illness that
affect a great proportion of our Veterans. In addition to the tremendous burden of suffering and economic costs,
these diseases increase the mortality rate among Veterans. Thus, this study is aimed at addressing the need for
understanding the pathophysiology, identifying key drivers, and testing novel approaches to genetically informed
customized treatment or prevention tailored to the individual characteristics of each patient.

title: Developing an integrated system for detailing the conformational flexibility, heterogeneity, and dynamics of functional oligonucleotides
text:
The proposed work will produce a powerful technology platform that opens the door to the study of structure
establishment by functional nucleic acids. The technology provides the solution to the unmet need to resolve
oligonucleotide structural transformations, co-existing solution structures, and conformer flexibility with ultra-high
sensitivity. Unleashing the true potential of structure establishment analyses for functional nucleic acids will
have an indelible impact on the development of new therapeutic strategies for diverse diseases.

title: Mechanisms and therapeutic potential of blocking the mitochondrial Mg2+ channel Mrs2 in obesity and NAFLD
text:
The most abundant divalent cation, Mg2+, is essential for cellular functions and perturbations are associated with
several clinical conditions, including obesity, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
(NAFLD), chronic kidney disease, and cancer; however, the molecular events that directly link Mg2+ to metabolic
disease progression are still elusive. Our proposed studies will reveal a previously unexplored mechanism linking
mitochondrial Mg2+ dynamics to key hepatic metabolic pathways, which may offer new therapeutic approaches
for the treatment of T2DM and comorbidities such obesity and NAFLD.

title: Peripheral and Central Pathways of α3 Glycine Receptors as Non-Opioid Molecular Targets to Treat Pain
text:
To address the current opioid crisis, a new class of potent non-opioid analgesics has been developed in the
investigators’ laboratories. These future drug candidates are designed to target brain circuits involving a family
of proteins called glycine receptors. The proposed investigations aim to elucidate the dual roles of the α3 subtype
of glycine receptors in alleviating chronic pain and at the same time inhibiting the reward circuits in the brain,
thereby reducing the risk of drug dependence and abuse potential.

title: The JNK2-NLRP3 nexus in atrial fibrillation and its anti-AF therapeutic potentials
text:
Excessive binge alcohol intake has been widely recognized as a strong risk factor for atrial fibrillation (AF),
[especially a significant AF trigger in the aging population]. While alcohol is known to enhance inflammation, the
ineffectiveness of anti-inflammation clinical therapies in clinical trials for AF patients demonstrates the urgent
need to understand the detailed underlying mechanisms of alcohol and inflammation-associated AF. This
proposal is designed to fill this knowledge gap by identifying stress-response c-Jun N-terminal kinase JNK2 as an
important nodal point in alcohol-provoked inflammation-associated AF development and the results from this
proposal will form a strong foundation toward achieving our long-term goal of developing novel therapies to treat and
prevent AF.

title: Northwestern University Center for Chromatin NanoImaging in Cancer (NU-CCNIC)
text:
U54 CENTER NARRATIVE
Despite rapid advances in new anti-cancer therapeutics, for many solid cancers complete remission is still rare.
In many cases, tumors eventually develop resistance to treatments. One of the major barriers to effective
therapeutics is likely to be potentiated by highly transcriptionally plastic cancer stem cells. In this U54
Northwestern University Center for Chromatin Nanoimaging in Cancer, we will develop, optimize, test, and
deploy new nanoimaging technologies, integrated with state-of-the-art molecular and computational methods, to
address some of the long-standing questions related to the origin of cancer stem cells and their ability to adapt
to chemotherapies. Addressing these fundamental knowledge and technology gaps may help identify new
therapeutic strategies that prevent tumor resistance to therapeutics and relapse after treatment.

title: Mechanisms of Somatic Mutation in Alzheimer's Disease Using Single Neuron Analysis
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative diseases involve a loss of brain function and brain
cells over time and eventually cause death, affecting one third of people over the age of 85. Recent research
has found that brain cells build up new mutations in the DNA (known as somatic mutations) in AD, which
appears to harm the brain cells. This proposal will test how somatic mutations are related to the progression of
AD in the brain, and how they are related to the buildup of misfolded proteins amyloid-β and tau.

title: PEDF-enriched Urine-derived Stem Cell Sheets for Corneal Wound Healing in Mustard Gas Injury
text:
Chemical agents such as mustard gas inflict severe eye injuries, leading to burns and vision loss. While pigment
epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) shows promise in protecting and repairing the cornea, its effectiveness is
hindered by its rapid breakdown. This project seeks to engineer sheets of stem cells derived from the patient's
own urine to provide a sustained release of PEDF, aiming to minimize chronic corneal scarring, stimulate limbal
stem cell regeneration, and ultimately restore vision following mustard gas exposure.

title: Role of hypoxia in CD8+ T cell exclusion and suppression in pancreatic cancer
text:
Pancreatic cancer is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States
by 2030, and is characterized by a dense, fibroinflammatory stroma and a hypoxic tumor microenvironment
which can contribute to immunosuppression. The goal of this proposal is to determine how hypoxia regulates
CD8+ T cell infiltration and function via macropahges and fibroblasts in pancreatic cancer. My studies will provide
new insight on the hypoxic regulation of tumor-stroma crosstalk leading to immune suppression, and inform the
optimal design of immunotherapies for pancreatic cancer.

title: Radiology Core
text: Neuroimaging is a fundamental method for investigating the development of the human brain and spine structure and function in typically and atypically developing populations. MR imaging is key to support the aims of Park- Reeves Chiari & Syringomyelia Center (PRCSC) and the four sub-projects within the proposal. The goals of the Radiology imaging core (RC) are to provide comprehensive MRI service to the different projects within the PRCSC to facilitate imaging data acquisition. The RC will coordinate the initial and follow up MRI scans across all projects and cores. This will include close coordination with the administrative and clinical cores, clinical teams, and the Center for Clinical Imaging Research (CCIR) to guarantee scheduling at the appropriate times. The RC will perform the required steps to ensure quality control of the MRI scanners using regular phantom test scans and scan protocol compliance checks. Further, the RC will cover the full extent of handling of the MR imaging data, including using state-of-the art archiving software for all the PRCSC neuroimaging services. On the input side this includes uploading, anonymizing, and securely storing the data using the Park-Reeves CSC Centralized Neuroimaging Data Archive (CNDA). On the output side this includes giving access of the data to the project investigators to maximize the quality and impact of the PRCSC research by center investigators and their collaborators, securely distributing the raw and processed data to the different sub-projects as needed. The RC will assist with the procedures for standardized processing of the data for future use by the different sub- projects of the proposal. This includes simple anatomical measures, but also sophisticated software pipelines for processing of fMRI and DBSI data. Finally, the RC will promote new methods for analyzing MRI data and will provide a range of consultative and analytic services that will help PRCSC investigators, including new and early- stage investigators, incorporate imaging into their research efforts.
